analysis.one_liner: Adds a voluntary prescription drug benefit to Medicare for seniors and disabled beneficiaries.
analysis.headline: Introduced in May 2000 with 34 Senate Democrats behind it, the Medicare prescription drug bill died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing, a markup, or a single vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have created a new Medicare benefit paying half the negotiated price of prescription drugs for seniors and disabled beneficiaries, with annual caps that rise from $2,000 to $5,000. It would have required the federal government to cover drug costs for low-income Medicare beneficiaries, created a $50 billion reserve fund for a future catastrophic drug benefit, extended full drug coverage to organ transplant patients, and paid employers to keep retiree drug plans alive. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in May 2000 and never heard from again before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who lacked drug coverage — the bill's own findings say at least two-thirds had unreliable, inadequate, or no coverage — along with low-income beneficiaries whose costs would have been covered by the government, organ transplant patients needing immunosuppressive drugs, and employers sponsoring retiree drug plans.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors and disabled people on Medicare

how_it_helps.text: Creates a voluntary Medicare drug program covering essentially all outpatient prescription drugs, with Medicare paying 50 percent of the negotiated price up to annual caps of $2,000 in 2002-2004, $3,000 in 2005-2007, $4,000 in 2008, and $5,000 in 2009.

The bill's own findings state that at least two-thirds of Medicare beneficiaries had unreliable, inadequate, or no drug coverage, and that uncovered seniors paid at least 15 percent more for drugs than people with coverage.

Requires the government to pay Medicare drug cost-sharing for qualified Medicare beneficiaries and for Medicare-eligible people with incomes between 100 and 150 percent of the poverty line, with 100 percent federal matching for those under 135 percent of poverty.
Extends comprehensive Medicare coverage of immunosuppressive drugs to all organ transplant patients, removing the time limit then in law.
Appropriates $50 billion to a catastrophic drug reserve fund and directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to propose a catastrophic drug benefit taking effect no later than January 1, 2003.
Pays employers two-thirds of the monthly premium for each retiree kept under an existing employer drug plan, to keep companies from dropping retiree coverage.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through appropriations equal to all enrollee premiums plus half of employer contributions, plus a $50 billion catastrophic reserve fund, and enrollees themselves, who pay half the monthly premium deducted from Social Security checks.

drawbacks.text: The federal contribution is an open-ended entitlement: the government must match every enrollee premium dollar and half of employer premium payments, with no overall spending cap, plus a $50 billion reserve fund.

The benefit starts at only a 50 percent coinsurance rate with a $2,000 annual cap in 2002, and the catastrophic protection is just a reserve fund and recommendations unless Congress separately enacts it — leaving high-cost patients exposed in early years.

The bill bars the Secretary from requiring a formulary, setting a price structure, or interfering with negotiations between private entities and drug manufacturers, so the government's enormous new purchasing power could not be used to negotiate drug prices directly.

Enrollment is generally limited to an initial period, with reenrollment restricted, so people who decline early face barriers later; the bill itself only commissions a study on whether annual open enrollment would be advisable.

A voluntary program funded half by premiums invites adverse selection — the people most likely to enroll are those with high drug costs — which pushes premiums up for everyone, a standard concern for such designs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have delivered a real, overdue benefit to a large group — most Medicare beneficiaries had no reliable drug coverage — and its low-income provisions were generous, with 100 percent federal matching. The honest costs are that taxpayers fund an open-ended new entitlement, early-year caps leave heavy cost-sharing, and the design deliberately gives up government negotiating leverage over drug prices by routing everything through privately contracted entities and barring price-setting. The late Senator Moynihan's generation of fiscal hawks would have flagged the financing; advocates would counter that the noninterference clause was the price of political viability. On balance it was a substantial, if imperfect, benefit for ordinary people.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate's Democratic leader introduced it in May 2000 with 33 Democratic cosponsors, but the Republican-chaired Finance Committee, to which it was referred, never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

narrative.text: Tom Daschle introduced the MEND Act in the Senate on May 10, 2000, joined by 33 Democratic cosponsors including the ranking members of key committees.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day.
The complete action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action ever taken after the referral.
The 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, and the bill expired with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, the existing market stayed intact: drug makers kept pricing power with no government negotiation, Medigap insurers kept selling expensive drug supplements, and seniors without coverage kept paying full price out of pocket. The millions of beneficiaries who lacked drug coverage gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers and insurers kept the status quo

for.name: Tom Daschle
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: 33 of 45 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it the entire Democratic conference minus a handful of members.

for.name: Daniel Patrick Moynihan
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as the senior Democrat on the committee with jurisdiction over Medicare.

against.name: William V. Roth Jr.
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee to which the bill was referred, never scheduled a hearing or markup on it, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill, and the Republican majority brought no Medicare drug bill of this design to the floor in 2000.

sides.party_line_note: All 34 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-chaired Finance Committee took no action after referral.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and private claims administrators
industries.note: The bill requires the drug benefit to be administered through competitively awarded contracts with private entities in at least 15 service areas, and bars the government from negotiating with drug makers directly. That makes private intermediaries the permanent channel through which a public benefit flows.

A new subsidized benefit would steer drug purchases from tens of millions of beneficiaries, and the bill's noninterference clause protects manufacturers from any government price-setting. The industry gains volume without pricing concessions, at taxpayer expense.

Pharmacies get guaranteed access to participation agreements, negotiated prices that apply to enrollees even after benefit limits are exhausted, and possible bonus payments in rural areas. The bill specifically requires studies of effects on independent and rural pharmacies.
The bill's findings call Medigap drug premiums too expensive for most beneficiaries, especially older seniors. An affordable Medicare drug option would pull customers away from that market.
The Employer Incentive Program pays sponsors two-thirds of the monthly premium for each retiree kept on an employer drug plan, subsidizing companies to maintain coverage they were cutting.
